title: School Newsroom: The Cafeteria Debate
subtitle: Civic Journalism & Policy Analysis
summary: Our middle school throws away about 120 pounds of food each day while students ask for fresher lunch choices. Interview the head chef, analyze waste and cost data, choose your next lead, record a balanced broadcast, and publish an editorial for the school board.

briefing.scene: The Lincoln Times editor has given you the cafeteria story. The school board votes next week on whether to change how lunch is served. Chef Martinez and Student Council president Mia Alvarez disagree about what should change, and both say the numbers are on their side.
briefing.goal: Find out what the evidence really shows, decide what else you need to check, report both sides fairly on the midday broadcast, and publish an editorial with a clear recommendation.

interview.title: Audio Interview: Chef Martinez and Student Council President Mia Alvarez

turns.speaker: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Welcome to the Lincoln Middle newsroom. Our question today: why does our cafeteria throw away about 120 pounds of food every school day? I'm here with Chef Martinez and Student Council president Mia Alvarez.

turns.speaker: Chef Martinez
turns.text: We would love to serve more fresh, local produce, but the federal reimbursement is only about four dollars per lunch tray, and that has to pay for the food, the workers, and the milk. Last Tuesday we served a fresh kale salad, and seventy percent of it ended up in the compost bin.

turns.speaker: Mia Alvarez
turns.text: I understand the budget, Chef, but students want a voice in the menu. When the Student Council helped design the stir-fry bowl bar in October, participation rose forty percent and plate waste dropped to under five pounds a day.

turns.speaker: Chef Martinez
turns.text: I'll admit the stir-fry bar worked. But federal rules require every tray to include a fruit or a vegetable, so we cannot just remove the salad. We have to find a way to make students want to eat it.

turns.speaker: Jordan Lee
turns.text: So maybe the question is not whether to change, but how. Mia, what would you ask the school board to do?

turns.speaker: Mia Alvarez
turns.text: Start a pilot. Let students build their own lunch at a station two days a week, and weigh the waste every Friday. If the numbers improve, expand it.

memo.title: Lincoln Middle School Cafeteria Waste Audit
text: The National School Lunch Program requires schools to offer vegetables from several groups each week, including dark green, red and orange, and beans and peas. Meals must also meet limits on calories and sodium. A school that ignores these rules can lose part of its federal reimbursement, so menus cannot be built only around what students request.

In October, the Lincoln Green Team weighed uneaten food for ten school days. Pre-plated broccoli produced an average of 42 pounds of waste per day. The self-serve salad station, where students chose their own portions, produced only 8 pounds per day, even though it served a similar number of students.

Waste also costs money. The district pays hauling fees for trash and compost, and every pound thrown away is food that was bought but never eaten. District managers estimate that a batch-cooked, build-your-own model would cut hauling fees by 18 percent. However, fresh produce costs about 12 percent more per tray at first, so the district should test the idea before expanding it.

director.title: Interview: District Nutrition Director
director.summary: The district nutrition director confirms that build-your-own stations are allowed as long as every tray still includes the required fruit or vegetable, so the federal rules are less of a barrier than the chef feared.

turns.speaker: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Dr. Whitfield, can a school let students build their own lunch and still follow the federal rules?

turns.speaker: Dr. Whitfield
turns.text: Yes. A serving line can be self-serve as long as each student takes the required parts of a meal, including a fruit or a vegetable. Many districts use signs and a cashier check to make sure every tray qualifies.

turns.speaker: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Does the district allow a trial at one school?

turns.speaker: Dr. Whitfield
turns.text: We do. A two-month pilot with weekly weigh-ins is exactly the kind of evidence the school board asks for before it changes a policy.

survey.title: Why Students Throw Food Away
survey.summary: In a survey of 240 Lincoln students, 36 percent said they threw food away because they did not like the taste and 31 percent said they did not have enough time to eat. Only 19 percent said they were not hungry.

chart.title: Main reason students threw food away (survey of 240 students)

pilot.title: Westbrook County Pilot Report
pilot.summary: A middle school in Westbrook County tested build-your-own lunch bowls for eight weeks. Daily waste fell from 95 to 52 pounds, and the cost per tray rose by only 9 cents.
text: Westbrook Middle School tested a build-your-own lunch bowl line for eight weeks last spring. Students chose a grain, a protein, and at least one vegetable, and a staff member checked every tray before the cashier.

Cafeteria workers weighed uneaten food every Friday. Before the pilot, the school threw away an average of 95 pounds of food per day. By week eight, that number had fallen to 52 pounds, a drop of 45 percent.

The cost per tray rose by only 9 cents, because the kitchen cooked in large batches and stopped throwing away pre-packaged vegetables. Principal Dana Whitlock said that the biggest surprise was participation: more students chose the hot lunch than before.

phases.title: Audio Interview: Chef Martinez and Mia
phases.instructions: Listen to the interview. Notice what limits the chef and what result Mia reports. Then answer two questions and pin the best evidence to your board.

tasks.q: According to Chef Martinez, what limits what the cafeteria can serve?

options.text: The kitchen does not have enough ovens to cook fresh food.
About four dollars per tray must cover food, workers, and milk.
Students refuse to eat any vegetables the kitchen serves.
Seventy percent of the kale salad ended up in the compost bin.

tasks.explain: Chef Martinez says "the federal reimbursement is only about four dollars per lunch tray, and that has to pay for the food, the workers, and the milk." The compost number is true, but it shows the result of waste, not the limit on the menu.

tasks.q: What does Chef Martinez's comment, "I'll admit the stir-fry bar worked," suggest about him?

options.text: He thinks student ideas cannot help the cafeteria improve any of its meals.
He has decided to end the federal lunch program.
He is open to changes when students are more likely to eat the food.
He agrees that the stir-fry bar was popular.

tasks.explain: After admitting the bar "worked," he adds, "We have to find a way to make students want to eat it." That shows he will change the menu when it reduces waste. Agreeing it was popular is true but stops short of his openness to change.

tasks.q: Choose the statements that support this claim: "Student choice can reduce cafeteria food waste."

pool.text: the federal reimbursement is only about four dollars per lunch tray
participation rose forty percent and plate waste dropped to under five pounds a day
seventy percent of it ended up in the compost bin
federal rules require every tray to include a fruit or a vegetable
I'll admit the stir-fry bar worked.
why does our cafeteria throw away about 120 pounds of food every school day

phases.title: Policy Memo, Waste Chart, and Cost Table
phases.instructions: Read the audit memo, then compare the waste chart with the cost table. Look for facts that both sources support.

tasks.q: According to the audit, what happened at the salad station where students chose their own portions?

options.text: Waste was only 8 pounds per day when students chose their own portions.
Waste was 42 pounds per day because students took far too much food at the station.
Hauling fees fell by 18 percent during the October audit.
Waste dropped, but only on days when broccoli was served.

tasks.explain: The memo says the self-serve salad station "produced only 8 pounds per day." The 42 pounds belongs to pre-plated broccoli, and the 18 percent hauling savings is an estimate for a future model, not an October result.

tasks.q: In the memo, what does "reimbursement" mean?

options.text: a rule about which foods students may bring from home to lunch
a fee the district pays to haul away trash
a limit on the calories and sodium in a meal
money paid back to a school for the meals it serves

tasks.explain: The memo says a school that ignores the rules "can lose part of its federal reimbursement." That only makes sense if reimbursement is money the government pays back for meals. Hauling fees and calorie limits appear nearby but mean something else.

tasks.q: Why do district managers want to test build-your-own stations before expanding them?

options.text: Federal rules forbid students from choosing their own foods in any cafeteria line.
Fresh produce costs more per tray at first, so they need proof the savings are real.
Students already dislike every vegetable the kitchen serves, so no change will ever help.
The Green Team found no waste at the salad station.

tasks.explain: The memo says fresh produce "costs about 12 percent more per tray at first, so the district should test the idea before expanding it." A test shows whether the lower hauling fees and waste really offset the higher food cost.

tasks.q: Which statement is supported by BOTH the waste chart and the cost table?

options.text: Pre-plated trays are cheaper and also produce less waste.
The district would save $225 a month in hauling fees.
Choice-based serving styles produced less waste but cost more per tray.
Student-designed stations would lower every cost the district pays, from food to hauling.

tasks.explain: The chart shows self-serve (8 pounds) and student-designed (4.5 pounds) stations wasting far less than pre-plated food (42 and 18 pounds). The table shows build-your-own costing $2.02 per tray versus $1.80. The $225 savings comes from the table alone, and food cost rises.

tasks.q: A board member says, "Switch every school to build-your-own stations next month." What is the strongest reason to answer "not yet"?

options.text: The audit compared different foods, so a pilot should weigh the same meals both ways.
Build-your-own costs more per tray, so it can never save the district any money at all.
The table shows hauling fees would rise by 18 percent.
Federal rules require every school in the district to keep serving pre-plated trays.

tasks.explain: The 42-pound and 8-pound figures compare broccoli with a salad station, which are different foods, so they do not prove the whole model works. The table estimates that hauling fees would fall by $225 a month, not rise, and the memo never says the rules require pre-plated trays.

tasks.q: Choose the sentences from the memo that support this claim: "Letting students serve themselves can reduce waste and cost."

pool.text: Meals must also meet limits on calories and sodium.
The self-serve salad station, where students chose their own portions, produced only 8 pounds per day
In October, the Lincoln Green Team weighed uneaten food for ten school days.
a batch-cooked, build-your-own model would cut hauling fees by 18 percent
Pre-plated broccoli produced an average of 42 pounds of waste per day.

phases.title: Choose Your Next Lead
phases.instructions: You have time for one more interview or report before the broadcast. Your choice unlocks new evidence. The other leads are summarized for you, so the broadcast and the editorial work whichever lead you follow.

decision.q: Your broadcast goes live at noon. Which lead do you follow before you write?

options.text: Interview the district nutrition director about the federal rules
options.consequence: Dr. Whitfield explains that self-serve lines are allowed if every tray still has a fruit or vegetable. The rules are less of a barrier than the chef feared, and a pilot is something the board expects.

board.label: Rules check
board.text: Build-your-own lines follow federal rules when every tray includes a fruit or vegetable.

options.text: Survey students about why they throw food away
options.consequence: Taste (36 percent) and time to eat (31 percent) were the top reasons. Only 19 percent said they were not hungry, so the problem is not the amount of food but whether students like it and have time for it.

board.label: Student voice
board.text: 36 percent of students said they throw food away because they do not like the taste.

options.text: Read a report about a pilot at another school district
options.consequence: Westbrook Middle School cut daily waste from 95 to 52 pounds in eight weeks, and the cost per tray rose by only 9 cents. You have real evidence that a pilot can work, though it is a different school.

board.label: Other schools
board.text: A pilot at Westbrook Middle School cut waste from 95 to 52 pounds per day.

phases.instructions: Plan your report with the five planner slots, then record 45 to 90 seconds. Report both sides fairly and use your board.

task.scenario: You are the anchor of the Lincoln Middle midday news broadcast. Students, teachers, and the principal listen in every classroom, and they have heard only rumors about the cafeteria debate.
task.prompt: Report both sides of the cafeteria debate in a balanced way. Compare Chef Martinez's budget limits with Mia's student-choice idea, use at least two numbers from the audit, and end by telling listeners what the newsroom will report next.

guided.model: Good afternoon, Lincoln Middle. Today we are investigating why our cafeteria throws away 120 pounds of food a day. On one side, Chef Martinez explains that fresh food is hard to afford, because the reimbursement is only about four dollars per tray. On the other side, Mia Alvarez argues that students should help plan the menu. When students designed the stir-fry bar, plate waste dropped to under five pounds. The audit shows that pre-plated broccoli produced 42 pounds of waste, while the self-serve salad station produced only 8. Next, the newsroom will find out whether a pilot could work at our school.

successCriteria: I give both sides fairly, without saying which side is right.
I use at least two numbers from the audit or interview.
I use a contrast word such as however or on the other hand.
I finish with what the newsroom will report next.

listenFor: Neutral language when describing each side
Contrast connectors (however, on the other hand, while)
Accurate use of 42 pounds versus 8 pounds
teacher.followUp: Which number in your report would a skeptical listener question first?

phases.title: Editorial: A Policy for the School Board
phases.instructions: Write an editorial that takes a position, uses evidence from at least two sources, answers one concern, and ends with a call to action.

task.title: Editorial for the School Board
task.scenario: The Lincoln Times will print your editorial next to the school board's agenda. Board members have asked student reporters to propose a cafeteria policy that is realistic about money and about nutrition rules.
task.prompt: Write an editorial that takes a position on how the cafeteria should change. Use evidence from at least two sources, answer one concern from the other side, and finish with a clear call to action for the board.

frames: First, the waste audit shows that ___, which means ___.
Second, the cost table estimates that ___. Furthermore, ___.
Therefore, the board should vote to ___.
guided.model:
The school board should approve a build-your-own pilot because it cuts waste without breaking the budget. First, the waste audit shows that pre-plated broccoli produced 42 pounds of plate waste a day, while the self-serve station produced only 8, which means students eat more when they choose.

Second, the cost table estimates that hauling fees would drop by $225 a month. Furthermore, the district would have proof before it changes every school.

Some people worry that fresh food costs more under a four-dollar reimbursement. However, the table shows the extra 22 cents per tray is smaller than the savings from throwing away less. Therefore, the board should vote to run a two-month pilot.

revisionPrompts.prompt: Replace a general statement with an exact number from the chart or the table.
After each number, add a sentence that says what it proves.
Use a transition such as however or furthermore to connect your paragraphs.
Replace the word 'good' or 'bad' with a more exact word such as sustainable or costly.

successCriteria: My position is clear in the first or second sentence.
I support it with at least two numbers from the sources.
I fairly state a concern from the other side and answer it.
I end with a call to action the board can vote on.

lookFor: A defensible position tied to specific numbers
A counterargument introduced with a contrast word
A closing action tied to the claim
commonIssues: Citing the 42-pound figure without comparing it to 8 pounds
Using persuasive slogans instead of evidence

teacherQuestions: Which two numbers from the sources were the most persuasive to you? Why does a number persuade more than an opinion?
How did the lead you chose in the Decision phase change your editorial? What might the other leads have changed?
Chef Martinez and Mia both had good points. How did you stay fair to both sides in your broadcast?
The 42-pound and 8-pound figures compare different foods. What would a stronger comparison look like?
debrief.connections: Connects to civics (how local boards make policy), math (comparing quantities and percents), and ELA (balanced reporting versus opinion writing). The claim-evidence-reasoning pattern also appears in the Watershed and Space Colony missions.
